newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS- Thai crisis could test Japan's resolve.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS- Thai crisis could test Japan's resolve.

text.p: An expected request by Thailand for Japanese participation in a multi-billion dollar financial rescue scheme could be the first real test of Tokyo's resolve to take the lead in promoting Asian financial stability.
Most analysts say Japan has no alternative to accepting a big part of the burden for easing Bangkok's credit crunch and preventing a chain reaction in the region.
"The fact is simple -- Japan has to pay most of the cost," said C.H. Kwan, a senior economist at the Centre for Policy Research at Nomura Research Institute.
"Just as in Mexico, the final burden fell to the United States and since the Mexican crisis, Japan started to think about that."
Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya arrives here next week for what he said on Thursday was a visit aimed mainly at building up ties with his Japanese counterpart.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Friday that Thailand had made no specific requests for help with its financial problems.
Thai officials said earlier this week, however, that Bangkok was studying the requirements and prospects of tapping multi-million dollar foreign loans to ease its credit crunch.
Thailand last week sent markets into a frenzy by announcing a de facto devaluation of its currency, sending the baht 15 to 20 percent lower with a surprise move to float the baht.

The baht fell to a record low of 29.75 to the dollar early on Friday in line with the Philippine peso, which was dragged down after Manila's central bank announced it would allow its currency to move in a wider range against the dollar.
Other Asian currencies were thrown into a tailspin by Manila's move, which dealers said did little to restore investors' fragile confidence in the region.

Japan, once cautious toward a more active role on the Asian monetary front, has recently altered that wary stance, in part due to efforts by the finance ministry's Eisuke Sakakibara, who on July 15 will take over as Tokyo's top financial diplomat.

Sakakibara, who will become vice finance minister for international affairs, was instrumental in bringing Japan into Asian repurchase pacts in which regional central banks agreed to help defend their currencies against speculative attacks.
The first test of the bilateral pacts came with the market's assault against the baht, but the arrangements proved insufficient to the task.

"The repo agreements basically only provide liquidity using U.S. treasuries as collateral, but the foreign exchange reserves of Thailand were falling and it was difficult to offer collateral," Kwan said.

Japan last month presented to the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations a plan to hold a meeting later this year for Asian emerging nations and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank on financial stability.
Efforts to work out a Thai rescue plan will be the first concrete test of Tokyo's willingness to shoulder economic leadership in the region.
"There are a lot of conservative elements who would rather not take responsibility and leave it to the IMF," said Ron Bevacqua, a senior economist at Merrill Lynch in Tokyo.
"But I don't think they have a choice. Ultimately there is too much at stake politically, economically and symbolically."
What form a Thai rescue package might take remains unclear, including the potential role of the IMF.
An IMF official said on Wednesday that there were no plans for a Mexico-style international aid package for the country.
And a finance ministry source said Japan could not play an IMF-like role in setting conditions for a rescue package but would cooperate in any plan led by the international body.
Some analysts said Japan was reluctant to usurp IMF leadership, partly from fear other Asian economies might line up for handouts.
"For Japan's government to enter into an agreement like the United States did for Mexico would establish a precedent they might not want to set," said one analyst.
But Tokyo could find itself in the hot seat if the IMF set conditions that Thailand felt were too strict.

"It's easier to enlist Japanese banks when it (the package) is IMF-led, but Thailand may not be willing to meet IMF conditions," a Japanese economist said. "It would be very difficult for the finance ministry to do it on its own, but they may have no choice."
